channel.title: torontotrees
channel.description: Essays and visualizations built on Toronto's open street-tree data.

item.title: The 61-centimetre line — what Toronto's new tree bylaw actually selects for
item.description: On September 1, 2026, Toronto starts protecting private trees over 61 cm across as "distinctive." Run that same line across the 689,013 city-owned street trees and it selects two things the bylaw never mentions: species the city regrets planting, and streets laid out before the car.

item.title: Tree bingo — three printable cards for a Toronto walk
item.description: Three difficulty-tiered tree-bingo cards (25 species each) you can print or screenshot and use on any walk through Toronto. Easy, medium, hard. Suitable for kids, adults, dog walks, transit commutes, and post-coffee dawdles.

item.title: The caterpillar test — why a Toronto oak is worth a hundred ginkgos
item.description: Doug Tallamy's research applied to Toronto: how many native insect species each genus on the city's planting list actually supports. Oaks support 534 species. Ginkgos support 3. The ecological gap between street trees you can't see by looking at them.

item.title: Three trees I can't explain — anomalies in Toronto's street-tree dataset
item.description: A 250-centimetre hawthorn that physically can't exist. 4,664 cherries the city can't tell apart. A single pawpaw on Macdonell Avenue. Three small mysteries from a 689,013-row dataset.

item.title: What Kyoto's monks know that Toronto's dataset doesn't
item.description: Yasuyuki Aono's 1,200-year cherry-blossom record from Kyoto and Toronto's 689,013-row street-tree inventory are the same idea — watch a city's trees — taken to opposite extremes. One species, twelve centuries vs. 303 species, one snapshot.

item.title: The densest 100 metres — Arlington Avenue and the city's most-treed block
item.description: Toronto's most tree-dense residential 100-metre cell is on Arlington Avenue between Winnett and Rushton, in Humewood-Cedarvale. 128 trees in a single block, 34 of them red oaks. A short walking tour of one block, and what it tells us about the city's quiet ecological turnaround.

item.title: The Norway-maple paradox — Toronto's most-planted tree is the one the city no longer plants
item.description: 99,931 Norway maples line Toronto's streets — 14.5% of the entire street-tree canopy and 26% of the mature trees. But under 2% of new saplings are Norway maples. The most successful planting program in Toronto history is now a 50-year passive removal.

item.title: The lilac week — on a flower that becomes a person
item.description: Lilacs are the most reliably memory-tied flower in North American family folklore. The species your great-grandmother had in her yard was almost certainly Syringa vulgaris — and the reason there isn't one on Toronto's streets is structural, not horticultural.

item.title: The narrow-street advantage — why Toronto's old grid carries 4× the trees of its new condos
item.description: The densest 200m stretch of street trees in Toronto has forty. The sparsest has three. The difference isn't income, care, or policy — it's whether the street was laid down before or after the car.

item.title: The ravines — the other half of Toronto's canopy
item.description: 689,013 city-owned street trees are on a map. An estimated 5 to 8 million more live in Toronto's 11,000 hectares of ravine, 17% of the city's land area. This post is about the canopy that doesn't appear on treeto.ca — and why.

item.title: A tale of two Victorians — Cabbagetown vs. Trinity-Bellwoods
item.description: Two old downtown Toronto neighbourhoods, same era, same rowhouse DNA, same gentrification arc. One has 45% canopy. The other has 20%. Here's what separated them.

item.title: Toronto's veteran street trees — a hall of fame
item.description: The single largest specimen of each of Toronto's 25 most common street-tree species — a 247-cm London plane, a 236-cm red oak, a 190-cm Dutch-elm-disease survivor, and 22 more. Each with a Street View link.

item.title: Toronto's street trees are worth $20 million a year
item.description: Applying published ecosystem-service equations to each of 686,000 Toronto street trees — totalling $20M/year in carbon, stormwater, air quality, and cooling benefits. And an 80× gap between neighbourhoods.

item.title: The west-end cherry belt — where to see cherry blossoms in Toronto
item.description: High Park is famous for cherry blossoms. But the data says Oakwood Village has more — and nine times as many cherries line the west-end blocks around St Clair.

item.title: Toronto's heat islands aren't where you'd expect
item.description: An impervious-minus-canopy heat proxy maps the city's hottest and coolest neighbourhoods. The hottest are the financial-district condo core — not the income-vulnerable neighbourhoods the equity narrative predicts.

item.title: The honey locust — Toronto's civic workhorse
item.description: Gleditsia triacanthos is Toronto's #2 tree by count and its #1 choice for new plantings today. 60,000 of them, mostly thornless-seedless cultivars engineered specifically for city life. And a new monoculture risk.

item.title: Beyond the curb — Toronto's actual canopy
item.description: Toronto's 2018 LiDAR land-cover data shows 25.9% canopy cover citywide. And it reveals that the inequity gap for street trees is three times larger than the gap for total canopy — meaning the city itself is the gap.

item.title: Every street tree in Toronto, as a dot
item.description: A pointillist portrait of Toronto: 689,013 city-owned street trees, coloured by genus. Plus a map showing just the 69,563 Norway maples — and why that matters.

item.title: Toronto's rarest street trees — a pilgrimage guide
item.description: Seven tree species have exactly one specimen in all of Toronto's city-owned street-tree inventory. Here's where to find them (with addresses).

item.title: The ginkgo — Toronto's 17,474 living fossils
item.description: Ginkgo biloba is the sole survivor of an entire plant division that predates dinosaurs. Toronto is quietly planting tens of thousands of them, almost all under 15 years old.

item.title: The black locust — Toronto's 2,943 Robinia pseudoacacia
item.description: Black locust is one of Toronto's most under-sung street trees: 2,943 of them, honey-scented flowers in early June, rot-proof wood, and a 182-cm specimen in Don Mills that's probably older than most of us.

item.title: A decade of standing still — how Toronto's canopy survived the ash catastrophe
item.description: Between 2008 and 2018, Toronto lost an estimated 80,000 mature ash trees to emerald ash borer. Over the same decade, citywide canopy cover went from 25.84% to 25.89%. Here's who paid the bill and who got the gain.

item.title: Toronto's canopy is unequally shared — torontotrees
item.description: Four findings from an afternoon with Toronto's 689,013 street trees: income vs. canopy, the Norway maple that city no longer plants, and downtown's honey-locust monoculture.

item.title: What the trees know
item.description: Between the data and the product is the reason. A reflection on Toronto's oldest street trees, what they've outlived, and the quieter kind of infrastructure they represent.
